problem: The trap says that using hg instead of hfg at 10 bar and x = 0.90 gives a value 'about 201 kJ/kg too high'. The 201 kJ/kg figure belongs to a different mistake: taking h = hg (the saturated-vapour value) as the mixture enthalpy, error 2778.1 − 2576.6 = 201.5. If a student really substitutes hg into the mixture formula, h = hf + x·hg = 762.8 + 0.90 × 2778.1 = 3263.1 kJ/kg, which is 3263.1 − 2576.6 = 686.5 kJ/kg too high, not 201. The headline and the number describe two different errors, so a student cannot tell which mistake is being warned against.
fix: Separate the two traps. (a) Taking h = hg for a wet mixture: at x = 0.90 this gives 2778.1 kJ/kg, about 201 kJ/kg too high. (b) Substituting hg in place of hfg: h = hf + x·hg = 3263.1 kJ/kg, about 686 kJ/kg too high, because x·hf is then counted an extra time. Both exceed the correct 2576.6 kJ/kg.

problem: The symbol x is already defined in Section 1 as quality, a mass fraction between 0 and 1. The interpolation formula reuses x for the known independent variable (T, P or h), so 'x' carries two meanings on the same page and a student may read quality into the interpolation arithmetic.
fix: Use a different letter for the interpolation variable, for example y = y₁ + (z − z₁)(y₂ − y₁)/(z₂ − z₁), where z is the known value (T, P or h) and y the wanted property; keep x only for quality.

problem: 'Using hg would count the liquid part twice' is loose. Using hg in h = hf + x·hg adds exactly x·hf extra, not the whole liquid enthalpy again; the phrase could be read as saying hf itself is doubled.
fix: Say: hg already contains hf, so writing h = hf + x·hg adds the liquid enthalpy hf once directly and x·hf again inside x·hg. The result is too high by x·hf.
